sections.title: The atom: nucleus, electrons, sizes, masses and charges

parts.title: Structure and numbers
parts.html:
An atom has a positively charged nucleus made of protons and neutrons, surrounded by negatively charged electrons. The nucleus is very much smaller than the atom — ten to a hundred thousand times smaller across — but contains almost all of its mass.

Sizes: an atom (and a small molecule) is about $1 \times 10^{-10}$ m across (0.1 nm); the nucleus about $1 \times 10^{-15}$ m. The 2022 report: converting 0.15 nm to $1.5 \times 10^{-10}$ m "was difficult" — nano is $10^{-9}$.

ParticleRelative massRelative chargeWhere
Proton1+1nucleus
Neutron10nucleus
Electronabout 1/1836 (negligible, ≈ 0.0005)−1orbiting the nucleus
Positronsame as an electron+1emitted in β⁺ decay

In a neutral atom the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the positive and negative charges cancel. The number of protons is what makes an element that element: every nucleus of a given element has the same positive charge.

parts.title: Why the atom is neutral
parts.question: A neutral atom of carbon has 6 protons. State how many electrons it has, and explain why the atom has no overall charge. (2 marks)
steps: Number: 6 electrons — in a neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
Why neutral: each proton has a charge of +1 and each electron −1, so 6 of each give a total charge of zero.

questions.text: Which statement about the nucleus is correct?
options: It is about the same size as the atom
It contains almost all the atom's mass and is positively charged
questions.explain: Protons and neutrons; tiny; positive; almost all the mass.

questions.text: State the relative mass and relative charge of a proton, a neutron and an electron. (3)
questions.model:
• Proton: mass 1, charge +1.
  • Neutron: mass 1, charge 0.
  • Electron: mass about 1/1836 (very small), charge −1.

questions.text: What is the typical size of an atom?
questions.explain: About 10⁻¹⁰ m (0.1 nm); the nucleus is about 10⁻¹⁵ m.

questions.text: The diameter of an atom is 0.15 nm. Write this in metres. Type the answer as 1.5e-10.
Compare a positron with an electron. (2)
questions.model:

  • Opposite charge: the positron is +1, the electron −1.

questions.text: Explain why an atom has no overall electric charge. (2)
questions.model:
• It has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
  • Each proton'$s +1$ charge is cancelled by an electron'$s -1$ charge, so the total is zero.

sections.title: Isotopes and nuclide notation

parts.title: A, Z and isotopes
parts.html:
$${}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} \qquad A = \text{mass (nucleon) number} = \text{protons} + \text{neutrons} \qquad Z = \text{atomic (proton) number} = \text{protons}$$

So neutrons = A − Z, and in a neutral atom electrons = Z. ${}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}$: 6 protons, 8 neutrons, 6 electrons.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same number of protons, same atomic number) with different numbers of neutrons (different mass numbers). ${}^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C}$ and ${}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}$ are isotopes of carbon. Because the nucleus of every atom of an element has the same positive charge (same Z), isotopes have the same electrons and the same chemical properties; they differ in mass and, often, in stability — the heavier isotope is frequently radioactive.

The June 2023 scheme (Q7(a)(i)) rejected every option that did not have the same atomic number as the given element: that is the whole test.

parts.title: Reading a nuclide
parts.question: Uranium-235 is written ²³⁵₉₂U. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom. (2 marks)
steps: Protons: Z = 92. Electrons: also 92 (neutral atom).

questions.text: State what is meant by isotopes. (2)
questions.model:
• Atoms of the same element — the same number of protons (atomic number)…
  • …with different numbers of neutrons (different mass numbers).

questions.text: Which nucleus is an isotope of ¹⁴₇N?
questions.explain: Same atomic number (7 = nitrogen), different mass number.

questions.text: How many neutrons are in a nucleus of ⁶⁰₂₇Co?
Explain why ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl have the same chemical properties but different masses. (2)
questions.model:
• Same number of protons (17), so the same number of electrons, which decide the chemistry.
  • Different numbers of neutrons (18 and 20), so different mass numbers.

questions.text: In the notation ᴬ_Z X, what does A stand for?
options: The number of protons plus neutrons (mass number)
questions.explain: A is the nucleon (mass) number; Z is the proton (atomic) number.

Define isotope in the mark-scheme form
Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties but different masses
sections.blurb: Every nucleus is written with its mass number on top and its atomic number below. Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but different mass numbers — same protons, different neutrons.

sections.title: Electrons: set orbits, absorbing and emitting, and ions

parts.title: Levels and ions
parts.html:
In an atom the electrons orbit the nucleus at different set distances — energy levels (the Bohr model, T1). An electron can only sit in one of these levels, not in between.

An electron moves to a higher orbit (further from the nucleus) when the atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation of the right energy. It falls back to a lower orbit by emitting electromagnetic radiation. This is why hot gases give out light of particular colours (and how fluorescence works, Topic 5).

If an outer electron gains enough energy it leaves the atom altogether. The atom now has more protons than electrons: it is a positive ion. Anything that knocks electrons out of atoms is ionising — alpha, beta and gamma radiation, X-rays and ultraviolet. The June 2024 scheme (Q8(b)): ionisation is the loss (or gain) of electrons from atoms; "knocking electrons out" accepted.

parts.title: Ionisation by an alpha particle
parts.question: An alpha particle passes close to an atom and the atom becomes a positive ion. Explain how. (2 marks)
steps: What happens: the alpha particle transfers energy to an outer electron, which leaves the atom (is knocked out).

Why positive: the atom now has more protons than electrons, so it has an overall positive charge — a positive ion. The alpha particle loses a little energy each time, which is why it is stopped by a few cm of air.

questions.text: Describe what happens to an electron in an atom when the atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation. (1)
questions.model: • The electron moves to a higher orbit / energy level (further from the nucleus).

questions.text: State what is meant by ionisation. (1)
questions.model: • An atom losing (or gaining) an electron, so that it becomes charged (an ion); for ionising radiation, electrons are knocked out leaving a positive ion.

questions.text: An atom emits electromagnetic radiation. Which has happened?
options: An electron has moved to a higher orbit
An electron has moved to a lower orbit
A proton has left the nucleus
The atom has gained an electron
questions.explain: Falling to a lower level releases energy as EM radiation.

questions.text: Explain how an atom can become a positive ion. (2)
questions.model:
• An outer electron gains enough energy (e.g. from ionising radiation) to leave the atom.
  • The atom is left with more protons than electrons, so it is positively charged.

questions.text: Why are alpha, beta and gamma called ionising radiation?
options: They have enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms, forming ions
They travel at the speed of light
questions.explain: Ionising = removes electrons from atoms.

checklist: State that electrons orbit at set distances (energy levels) from the nucleus
Describe how absorbing or emitting EM radiation moves an electron between orbits
Explain how an atom becomes a positive ion, and link it to ionising radiation
sections.blurb: Electrons sit in orbits at set distances from the nucleus. They move up when they absorb electromagnetic radiation and down when they emit it; knock one out altogether and you have a positive ion — which is what ionising radiation does.

sections.title: Alpha, beta, gamma (and neutrons)

Radiation is emitted from unstable nuclei in a random process: you cannot say which nucleus will decay next or when (N7). All of alpha, β⁻, β⁺ and gamma are ionising.

Why penetration and ionisation are opposites: an alpha particle is large and carries +2, so it ionises almost every atom it passes, losing its energy within a few centimetres. A gamma ray has no charge and no mass, so it rarely interacts — it ionises little and travels far. The June 2024 scheme (Q8(a)): the charge on an alpha particle is +2.

"Alpha is stopped by paper" scores, and so does a comparison in the right dimension — "alpha is more ionising than gamma" was a mark on its own in June 2019 (Q8(a)(ii)). "Strongest" or "weakest" names neither dimension: write least penetrating / most ionising.

parts.title: Comparing two radiations
parts.question: Compare alpha and gamma radiation. (4 marks)
steps: Nature: alpha is a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons, charge +2); gamma is an electromagnetic wave with no mass or charge.
Ionising: alpha is strongly ionising; gamma is weakly ionising.
Penetration: alpha travels a few cm in air and is stopped by paper; gamma travels far and is only reduced by thick lead.

Effect on the nucleus (what the June 2025 6-marker wanted): alpha emission reduces the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2 — a new element; gamma emission changes neither — the nucleus just loses energy.

Read the bullets. When the question says "the processes of decay … what each radiation is and the effect on the original nucleus" (Nov 2021 Q9(d)), penetration and ionisation were ignored — every mark was for the nature (particle or wave, how many particles, charge) and the change in A and Z. June 2025 Q9(c) did credit them as a third strand. Write the nature and the nucleus first; add penetration only if there is room.

questions.text: State what an alpha particle, a beta particle and a gamma ray each consist of. (3)
questions.model:
• Alpha: a helium nucleus — two protons and two neutrons.
  • Beta(-minus): a fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus.
  • Gamma: electromagnetic radiation (a high-frequency wave).

questions.text: A source is placed near a detector. The count falls to background when a sheet of paper is put in the way. What is the source emitting?
questions.explain: Only alpha is stopped by paper.

questions.text: Which radiation is the most ionising?
questions.explain: Big, slow and doubly charged: alpha ionises most and penetrates least.

questions.text: Explain why alpha radiation is strongly ionising but only travels a few centimetres in air. (2)
questions.model:
• It is relatively large and has a +2 charge, so it pulls electrons off almost every atom it passes — strongly ionising.
  • Each ionisation transfers some of its energy, so it soon loses all its energy and stops.

questions.text: What is the charge on an alpha particle?
questions.explain: Two protons, no electrons: +2.

questions.text: A source emits beta and gamma radiation. Describe how you could show, using absorbers and a detector, that it emits both. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1BaselinePlace the source a fixed distance in front of the GM tube (not "in" it — June 2018 Q3(a)); measure the count rate with nothing in the way, for the same time each reading, and subtract the background.
2AluminiumPut a few mm of aluminium between source and detector, keeping the source–tube distance the same: the count falls but does not reach background — the aluminium absorbs the beta particles so fewer reach the tube (Nov 2021 Q3(c)(i)); something more penetrating remains.

sections.title: Background radiation and how radiation is detected

parts.title: Where it comes from, how it is detected
parts.html:
Background radiation is the low-level ionising radiation that is always present in the environment, from natural and artificial sources.

From the EarthFrom spaceArtificial
radon gas from rocks and soil (the largest share in the UK); rocks and building materials (granite); food and drink (potassium-40 in bananas, Brazil nuts)cosmic rays — high-energy particles from the Sun and beyond, more at altitude and in aircraftmedical X-rays and scans (the largest artificial share); nuclear industry and weapons-test fallout (tiny)

Detecting it. A Geiger–Müller (GM) tube with a counter: each ionising particle or ray entering the tube ionises the gas inside, giving a pulse of current that is counted — the reading is a count rate in counts per second or per minute. Photographic film is darkened (fogged) by ionising radiation, the more radiation the darker — film badges worn by radiographers show the dose they have received.

Measuring the background count (June 2024 Q8(c), 3 marks): use a GM tube and counter with no source nearby; count for a measured time (several minutes, because the counts are random); divide counts by time; repeat and average. Then subtract it from every reading taken with a source: corrected count rate = measured count rate − background count rate.

parts.title: Correcting a count
parts.question: With no source present a GM tube records 90 counts in 5 minutes. With a source in place it records 420 counts per minute. Calculate the corrected count rate of the source.
steps: Background rate: $90 \div 5 = 18$ counts per minute.
Corrected: $420 - 18 = 402$ counts per minute. (Subtracting 90 instead of 18 — mixing counts with counts per minute — is the common slip.)

questions.text: State what is meant by background radiation, and give two natural sources. (3)
questions.model:
• Low-level ionising radiation that is always present in the environment.
  • Source 1: radon gas from rocks / rocks and soil / food and drink.
  • Source 2: cosmic rays from space.

questions.text: Which is the largest source of background radiation for most people in the UK?
questions.explain: Radon seeping from rocks and soil is about half the UK average dose; medical is the biggest artificial source.

questions.text: Describe how to measure the background count rate in a laboratory. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1EquipmentUse a GM tube and counter with no radioactive sources nearby.
2CountRecord the number of counts in a measured time (several minutes) and divide by the time.
3RepeatRepeat (in different places / times) and calculate a mean, because the counts arrive at random.

questions.text: The background count rate is 20 counts per minute. A source gives a reading of 260 counts per minute. Calculate the corrected count rate.
Describe how photographic film can be used to monitor the radiation dose of a hospital worker. (2)
questions.model:
• The film is worn in a badge; ionising radiation darkens (fogs) the film.
  • When developed, the darker the film the greater the dose received; windows of different absorbers show which type of radiation.

questions.text: Explain why readings of a weak source should be taken over a long time and repeated. (2)
questions.model:
• Decay (and background) is random, so the count in a short time varies a lot from one measurement to the next.
  • A long count and a mean of repeats averages out the random variation and gives a more accurate count rate.

sections.title: Decay equations: what each decay does to A and Z

parts.title: The five decays
parts.html:
DecayWhat happens in the nucleusMass number AAtomic number ZEquation pattern
Alpha α2 protons + 2 neutrons leave as a helium nucleus−4−2${}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} \rightarrow {}^{A-4}_{Z-2}\mathrm{Y} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$
Beta-minus β⁻a neutron turns into a proton and an electron; the electron is emitted0+1${}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{Y} + {}^{\;0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$
Beta-plus β⁺a proton turns into a neutron and a positron; the positron is emitted0−1${}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z-1}\mathrm{Y} + {}^{0}_{+1}\mathrm{e}$
Gamma γthe nucleus rearranges and loses energy as an EM wave, often just after another decay00${}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X}^{*} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} + \gamma$
Neutron emissiona neutron leaves−10${}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} \rightarrow {}^{A-1}_{Z}\mathrm{X} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}$

Balancing: the top numbers add up on both sides, and so do the bottom numbers. ${}^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$: 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2. For beta-minus, ${}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C} \rightarrow {}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{\;0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$: 14 = 14 + 0 and 6 = 7 + (−1).

Two things the examiners' reports pick out. β⁺ is not just β⁻ in reverse — think it through: in June 2025 "a common error was to describe beta-minus emission" when β⁺ was asked — a proton becomes a neutron and a positron is emitted, so Z goes down by one. And the beta symbol needs its charge: the June 2024 scheme gave a mark for writing β with −1, and a mark for numbers that balance.

Gamma after a decay (6.21): a nucleus that has just emitted an alpha or beta particle is often left with spare energy; it rearranges and gets rid of that energy as a gamma ray. Nothing about A or Z changes.

parts.question: Strontium-90 (⁹⁰₃₈Sr) decays by beta-minus emission to yttrium (Y). Write the nuclear equation and describe what happens inside the nucleus. (3 marks)

Inside: a neutron changes into a proton and an electron, and the electron is emitted at high speed.

questions.text: Describe the process of beta-plus decay. (2)

  • So no protons or neutrons leave and the element does not change — the nucleus rearranges, loses energy and becomes more stable (Nov 2021 Q9(c): any one of those three).

sections.title: Activity and half-life
equations: \text{half-life: time for activity (or undecayed nuclei) to halve}

parts.title: Definitions, and why activity falls
parts.html:
Activity is the number of decays per second of a source; its unit is the becquerel (Bq): 1 Bq = 1 decay per second. A GM tube measures a count rate, which is a fraction of the activity (it only catches the radiation that enters the tube).

The activity decreases over time because each decay uses up one unstable nucleus, so there are fewer undecayed nuclei left to decay; fewer nuclei → fewer decays per second.

Half-life is the time taken for half of the undecayed nuclei to decay — equivalently, the time for the activity (or count rate) to fall to half its value. Either form is credited; give one in full.

Random but predictable: it cannot be predicted when a particular nucleus will decay — each decay is random. But a source contains an enormous number of nuclei, and with large numbers the random behaviour averages out, so the half-life lets you predict how the activity of the whole source will fall. Like dice: you cannot say which die will show a six, but with a thousand dice about a sixth will.

The calculation types below do the four standard calculations: fraction remaining after n half-lives (1/2ⁿ), activity after a time, time taken for the activity to fall to a value, and reading a half-life from a decay graph (draw the horizontal line at half the activity, drop to the time axis — the June 2024 scheme gave one mark for the line at 48–52 Bq and one for the time read off).

parts.title: Activity after three half-lives
parts.question: A source has an activity of 800 Bq and a half-life of 6 hours. Calculate its activity after 18 hours.
steps: Number of half-lives: $18 \div 6 = 3$.
Halve three times: $800 \rightarrow 400 \rightarrow 200 \rightarrow 100$ Bq.
(Or: fraction left $= \dfrac{1}{2^{3}} = \dfrac{1}{8}$; $800 \times \dfrac{1}{8} = 100$ Bq.)

questions.text: State what is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope. (1)
questions.model: • The time taken for half the undecayed nuclei to decay (or for the activity to fall to half its original value).

questions.text: State what is meant by the activity of a source, and give its unit. (2)
questions.model:
• The number of decays per second (rate of decay).
  • Unit: the becquerel, Bq (1 Bq = 1 decay per second).

questions.text: Explain why the activity of a radioactive source decreases with time. (2)
questions.model:
• Each decay leaves one fewer undecayed (unstable) nucleus.
  • The activity depends on the number of undecayed nuclei, so as they are used up fewer decay each second.

questions.text: Radioactive decay is random, yet half-lives can be used to make predictions. Explain. (2)
questions.model:
• It cannot be predicted when any particular nucleus will decay.
  • But a source contains a very large number of nuclei, so the overall behaviour averages out and the half-life predicts how the activity of the whole sample changes.

questions.text: A source has an activity of 6000 Bq and a half-life of 8 days. Calculate its activity after 24 days.
The activity of a source falls from 1200 Bq to 150 Bq in 45 minutes. Calculate its half-life.
walkthrough: $1200 \rightarrow 600 \rightarrow 300 \rightarrow 150$: three half-lives in 45 min, so one half-life $= 15$ min.

questions.text: After two half-lives, what fraction of the original undecayed nuclei remain?
questions.explain: ½ × ½ = ¼. The source never quite reaches zero.

checklist: Define activity and its unit, and half-life in both forms
Explain why decay is random but the half-life is predictable
Carry out half-life calculations: fraction left, activity after n half-lives, time taken, and from a graph
sections.blurb: The activity of a source falls over time because there are fewer undecayed nuclei left. The half-life is how long it takes to halve — the same however much you start with, and the one thing about a random process that can be predicted.

sections.title: Dangers, precautions, contamination and irradiation

parts.title: Dangers
parts.html:
Ionising radiation knocks electrons out of atoms in living cells. That can damage or kill cells (high doses: radiation burns, radiation sickness) or damage the DNA in a cell so that it mutates; a mutated cell that keeps dividing is cancer. Write mutation and cancer — "it is dangerous" or "it makes you ill" score nothing.

Precautions when handling a source: keep it in a lead-lined box; handle it with tongs, never fingers, and point it away from people (distance); limit the time of exposure; use shielding (lead); don't eat or drink nearby; wash hands afterwards.

Medical staff and patients (6.31): staff wear film badges to monitor their dose, stand behind lead screens or leave the room, wear lead aprons, and limit their time — they are exposed every day, so their total dose would otherwise be high. Patients have dose limits: use the lowest dose that works, a short half-life tracer, and only when the benefit outweighs the risk. The 2022 report: two precautions must be different kinds — "gloves and masks" scored one, because gloves are protective clothing and masks (and goggles) are ignored; protective clothing and shielding or limited time or distance scored two. Lead was credited; aluminium ignored.

parts.title: Contamination and irradiation

IrradiationContamination

Does it make you radioactive?NoYes — the source is now in or on you

The June 2024 scheme (Q4(c), 2 marks): irradiation does not make the object radioactive; it can be stopped by shielding; the source is outside; it stops when the source is removed; "you can move away from irradiation" accepted.

parts.title: Comparing the hazards
parts.question: Explain why an alpha source is more dangerous inside the body than outside it. (3 marks)
steps: Outside (irradiation): alpha particles are stopped by the skin (or a few cm of air), so they cannot reach living cells inside — little harm.
Inside (contamination): the source is next to living cells, and alpha is the most strongly ionising radiation, so all its energy is absorbed in a small volume of tissue.
Consequence: many cells are damaged or mutated (risk of cancer), and the source cannot be shielded or removed once inside.

questions.text: Describe the dangers of ionising radiation to the body. (2)
questions.model:
• It ionises atoms in cells, which can kill or damage cells (tissue damage, burns).
  • It can damage DNA and cause mutations, which may lead to cancer.

questions.text: A technician injects patients with a radioactive tracer. State two different precautions that reduce the technician's exposure. (2)
questions.model:
• Shielding: lead apron / lead screen / keep the source in a lead container.
  • Limit the time near the source / increase the distance (tongs, stand back) / film badge to monitor the dose. (Two different kinds of precaution.)

questions.text: State the difference between contamination and irradiation. (2)
questions.model:
• Contamination: radioactive material is on or in the object (it becomes radioactive).
  • Irradiation: the object is exposed to radiation from an external source and does not become radioactive; it stops when the source is removed.

questions.text: Food is irradiated with gamma rays to kill bacteria. Does the food become radioactive?
options: No — irradiation does not make the object radioactive
questions.explain: Irradiation = exposure; no radioactive material is left in the food.

questions.text: Explain why gamma sources are more hazardous than alpha sources for irradiation, but alpha sources are more hazardous for contamination. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1IrradiationGamma penetrates the skin and reaches internal organs; alpha is stopped by the skin, so from outside it does little harm.
2ContaminationOnce inside the body, alpha is the most ionising, so it does the most damage to the cells around it.
3LinkGamma, being weakly ionising, mostly passes out of the body; and an internal source cannot be shielded.

questions.text: Give two precautions that limit the radiation dose to a patient having a tracer scan. (2)
questions.model:
• Use a tracer with a short half-life so the activity falls quickly after the scan / use the smallest activity that gives a clear image.
  • Only scan when the benefit outweighs the risk; keep a record of the patient's total dose (dose limits).

sections.title: How and why the model of the atom changed

parts.title: Three models and the evidence
parts.html:
1. Plum pudding (Thomson, after discovering the electron): the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons dotted through it like plums in a pudding. Mass and charge spread evenly.

2. Rutherford's nuclear model (from Geiger and Marsden's experiment):

ObservationConclusion
most alpha particles passed straight through the foil undeflectedthe atom is mostly empty space
some were deflected through small anglesthe centre of the atom is positively charged (repels the positive alpha particles)
very few (about 1 in 8000) were deflected back through more than 90°the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus

The plum pudding model could not explain this: if the positive charge were spread out thinly, nothing could turn an alpha particle round. So the model changed to a small positive nucleus with electrons orbiting far outside it. (The June 2022 scheme, Q8(b)(ii), gave a mark each for three observations — most pass straight through, some deflected through small angles (less than 90°), very few through large angles (more than 90°) — and three conclusions — mostly empty space, there must be a nucleus, which is small / dense / positive. "Bounce back" and "repelled" were allowed; "refracted" and anything about electrons ignored.)

3. Bohr: electrons orbiting freely would spiral into the nucleus, and hot gases emit light only at particular frequencies. Bohr proposed that electrons can only occupy certain fixed orbits (energy levels) at set distances, and move between them by absorbing or emitting fixed amounts of EM radiation. This agreed with experiment, so it replaced the free-orbit picture. Later, the nucleus was found to contain protons and (Chadwick, 1932) neutrons.

The pattern for the 6-marker: for each step say the model, the evidence, and why the evidence could not be explained by the old model.

parts.title: Observation to conclusion
parts.question: In the alpha-scattering experiment, a very small number of alpha particles were deflected straight back. Explain what this showed about the atom. (2 marks)
steps: Mass and charge concentrated: to turn a fast, heavy alpha particle round, it must have met something with a large positive charge and a large mass concentrated in a very small volume — a nucleus.
Tiny: because so few were deflected back, that nucleus must be very small compared with the atom — most alpha particles never came near it.

questions.text: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom. (2)
questions.model:
• A ball (sphere) of positive charge…
  • …with negative electrons embedded throughout it.

questions.text: In the alpha-scattering experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. Explain what this showed. (1)
questions.model: • The atom is mostly empty space.

questions.text: Explain why the results of the alpha-scattering experiment meant the plum pudding model had to be replaced. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1PredictionIn the plum pudding model the positive charge is spread out, so alpha particles should all pass through with little or no deflection.
2ObservationBut some were deflected through large angles and a few came straight back.
3New modelThat needs the positive charge and most of the mass to be concentrated in a tiny nucleus — the nuclear model.

questions.text: Describe how the Bohr model changed the nuclear model, and why. (2)
questions.model:
• Electrons are in fixed orbits (energy levels) at set distances from the nucleus, and move between them by absorbing or emitting EM radiation.
  • Because this agreed with experimental observations (e.g. atoms emit light only at particular frequencies) that free orbits could not explain.

questions.text: Which observation showed that the nucleus is positively charged?
options: Most alpha particles passed straight through
Some alpha particles were deflected away from the nucleus
questions.explain: Positive alpha particles repelled by a positive nucleus are deflected.

questions.text: A student models alpha scattering by rolling marbles at a heavy weight hidden under a sheet of paper. Give two limitations of this model. (2)
questions.model:
• The marble and weight have no charge, so the deflection is by contact rather than electrostatic repulsion; the model is not to scale (the weight is far too big compared with the atom).
  • It is two-dimensional (not 3D) / there is only one marble and one weight / all the marbles have the same speed, whereas alpha particles do not (June 2022 Q8(c)(ii)).

sections.title: Choosing a source: type and half-life, with reasons
equations: \text{half-life} \leftarrow \text{how long it must last / how soon it must be gone}

parts.title: The two-reason answer, and the half-life trap
parts.html:
Type: does the radiation need to get out of something (gamma: out of the body, through packaging, through soil)? Be partly stopped (beta: thickness gauge)? Stay inside a small space and ionise strongly (alpha: smoke alarm, internal cancer treatment)?

Half-life — and link it to the job, every time. The June 2022 report (kidney scan, 6-hour tracer): "too fast / too slow" scored nothing on its own; the credited answers were "with a 6-minute half-life the technician would not be able to take a reading (in 30 minutes)" and "with a 6-day half-life the patient would be exposed for a long time". The June 2023 scheme (RTG on a Mars rover): "long half-life" + a reason — the mission lasts years, the source cannot be replaced.

Half-lifeActivity behaviourDanger (6.30)Suits
short (minutes–days)very active now, gone soonhigh dose rate while it lasts, but it does not stay radioactivemedical tracers, PET, leak detection
long (years–millennia)steady low activity for a long timelow dose rate but the hazard lasts — waste must be stored for thousands of yearssmoke alarms, gauges, RTGs, dating

Precautions follow the half-life: a short half-life source needs heavy shielding and distance now; a long half-life source needs secure, long-term storage and keeping out of the environment (contamination).

parts.title: A tracer
parts.question: Technetium-99m emits gamma rays and has a half-life of 6 hours. Explain why it is suitable as a medical tracer. (4 marks)
steps: Type — gets out: gamma penetrates body tissue, so it can be detected outside the body by a gamma camera.
Type — low damage: gamma is weakly ionising, so it does little damage to cells on its way out.
Half-life — long enough: 6 hours gives time to inject it, let it reach the organ and take the scan.
Half-life — short enough: the activity has fallen to a safe level within a day or two, so the patient's dose is limited.

questions.text: A hospital has tracers with half-lives of 6 minutes, 6 hours and 6 days. Explain why the 6-minute and 6-day sources are unsuitable for a scan that takes 30 minutes. (2)
questions.model:
• 6 minutes: the activity would have fallen too far for a reading to be taken (five half-lives in 30 min — 1/32 left) by the time the scan is done.
  • 6 days: the patient would be left radioactive / exposed for days after the scan — an unnecessarily large dose.

questions.text: A radioactive source powers a space probe for a 20-year mission. Explain two properties the source should have. (2)
questions.model:
• A long half-life, so its activity (and power output) stays high for the whole mission — it cannot be replaced in space.
  • An alpha emitter (or one with high energy per decay), because alpha is easily absorbed to produce heating and needs little shielding; also high melting point / not chemically reactive.

questions.text: Which source would you choose to check the thickness of aluminium sheet (a few mm thick)?
questions.explain: Beta is fully stopped by a few mm of aluminium, so gamma (partly absorbed by metal) is needed; a long half-life keeps the reading steady. For paper it would be beta.

questions.text: Explain why a source with a short half-life can be more dangerous in the short term but less dangerous in the long term than one with a long half-life. (2)
questions.model:
• Short half-life: a high activity (many decays per second) at first, so a high dose rate now — but it soon decays away.
  • Long half-life: a lower activity now, but it stays radioactive for years, so the hazard (and the need to store it securely) lasts.

questions.text: Explain why alpha sources are not used as medical tracers. (2)
questions.model:
• Alpha is stopped by a few cm of tissue, so it could not be detected outside the body.
  • It is strongly ionising, so inside the body it would damage cells near the source.

questions.text: Explain the precautions needed for storing waste with a very long half-life. (2)
questions.model:
• It stays radioactive for thousands of years, so it must be stored securely for a very long time (sealed, deep underground, in stable rock).
  • It must be kept from contaminating water and soil, and shielded so it does not irradiate people.

checklist: Choose the type of radiation for a use from its penetration and ionising power, and say why
Choose a half-life for a use and say why, linked to the use
Explain why the danger of a source depends on its half-life
sections.blurb: "Explain why this source is suitable" is marked on reasons, not on naming the right source. Two reasons every time: one for the type of radiation (penetration, ionisation) and one for the half-life (long enough, short enough), each linked to the job.

sections.title: Half-life the hard way: background, graphs and working backwards

parts.title: The extra steps
parts.html:
Background in a graph. A measured count rate never falls to zero — it levels off at the background. Find the background from the flat tail, subtract it from the starting count to get the corrected count, halve that, add the background back, and read the time at which the measured curve reaches it. For the graph below: measured 180, background 20, corrected 160 → half is 80 → measured 100 → at $t = 20$ min. Halving 180 to 90 gives the wrong half-life (about 24 min).

Working backwards. If the activity is 50 Bq after 3 half-lives, the original was $50 \times 2^{3} = 400$ Bq. The June 2025 report (fluorine-18 curve): the common error was "using the original mass as 60.0 mg" — read the actual starting value off the graph.

Fractions and percentages. After $n$ half-lives the fraction left is $\dfrac{1}{2^{n}}$: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 → 50%, 25%, 12.5%, 6.25%. The fraction that has decayed is 1 minus that. "After how many half-lives is the activity below 10%?" → 4 (6.25%). A ratio question ("activity of A to B") is $2^{n}$ to 1.

Reading the graph in the exam: draw the horizontal line at half the (corrected) value, drop a vertical to the axis, label it. The June 2024 scheme gave a mark for the horizontal line and a mark for the time — show both.

Half of that: 80 counts/min from the source, which is a measured count of $80 + 20 = 100$ counts/min.
Read the time: the curve reaches 100 counts/min at $t = 20$ minutes. Half-life = 20 min.
Check: next halving: source 40 → measured 60 at $t = 40$ min ✓

sections.title: Contamination, irradiation and precautions: the explain marks
equations: \text{which? why? for how long? which radiation is worst?}

parts.title: The answers that score
parts.html:
Irradiation vs contamination — the June 2024 marks: irradiation does not make the object radioactive; it stops when the source is removed (you can move away); the source is outside; it can be shielded. Contamination: the source is on or in the object, which keeps emitting radiation, it is hard to remove, and it cannot be shielded from the inside.

Which radiation is worst? For irradiation from outside, gamma (and beta) — they penetrate to living tissue; alpha is stopped by skin. For contamination inside the body, alpha — all of its strongly ionising energy is absorbed by the surrounding cells. Dust and gas (radon) are the usual contaminants because they are breathed in.

Precautions, by situation (give different kinds):

WhoPrecautions
School labtongs, point the source away, lead-lined box, short exposure, no eating, wash hands
Radiographer / technicianlead apron or lead screen, leave the room, limit time, film badge (dose monitored), keep distance, rotate duties
Nuclear-industry workerfull protective suit and breathing apparatus against contamination, remote handling, dose monitoring, shielding
Patientlowest activity that works, short half-life, benefit outweighs risk, dose limits recorded

Why staff but not the patient? The patient has one scan; the technician does many every day, so their total dose would otherwise be far higher. That sentence is usually a mark.

parts.title: Contamination from radon
parts.question: Radon is a radioactive gas that seeps from the ground into some houses. Explain why breathing radon is more hazardous than being near a sealed gamma source of the same activity. (3 marks)
steps: Contamination: breathing radon puts the radioactive material inside the lungs — the body is contaminated, and the source stays there emitting.
Alpha inside: radon decays by alpha emission, which is strongly ionising, so all its energy is absorbed by the lung tissue around it, damaging and mutating cells.
Irradiation outside: the sealed gamma source only irradiates: gamma is weakly ionising, much passes straight through, and the exposure stops when you move away or shield it.

questions.text: Explain why a radiographer leaves the room while a patient is X-rayed, but the patient does not need protecting from the same exposure. (2)
questions.model:
• The radiographer would be exposed to many X-rays every day, so their total dose (and risk of cell damage / cancer) would be high.
  • The patient has one exposure, kept to the lowest useful dose, and the benefit of the diagnosis outweighs the small risk.

questions.text: A worker's overalls become contaminated with radioactive dust. Explain why this is more serious than the worker having been irradiated by the same source. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1ContinuesThe dust keeps emitting radiation, so the exposure continues after the worker leaves the area — irradiation would have stopped.
2Spread / insideThe dust can be breathed in or swallowed, putting the source inside the body where it cannot be shielded.
3AlphaInside the body even alpha (harmless from outside) does serious damage, as it is strongly ionising.

questions.text: Which is the best way to protect someone from a gamma source across a room?
options: Move further away and put a lead screen between
questions.explain: Gamma: distance and dense shielding. Gloves protect against contamination, not irradiation.

questions.text: Give three precautions a teacher should take when demonstrating a radioactive source in class, and say which hazard each reduces. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1DistanceHandle with tongs / keep the source at arm's length and pointed away — reduces the dose from irradiation (intensity falls with distance).
2Time / shieldingKeep it out of the lead-lined box for as short a time as possible — less exposure; the box shields it when stored.
3ContaminationDo not touch the source, eat or drink; wash hands — prevents contamination.

questions.text: Explain why a patient given a radioactive tracer is advised to keep away from young children for a day. (2)
questions.model:
• The patient is contaminated — the tracer inside them keeps emitting gamma rays, so they irradiate people nearby.
  • Children's dividing cells are more at risk from radiation; after a day the short-half-life tracer has largely decayed away.

sections.title: Treating tumours: internal and external radiation
equations: \text{external: gamma / X beams from several directions}
\text{internal: a source placed in the tumour (short-range, or sealed gamma)}

parts.title: The comparison
parts.html:
External (radiotherapy)Internal (brachytherapy, radioactive implants, injected isotopes)
Howbeams of gamma or X-rays from a machine outside the body, aimed at the tumour; the beam (or the patient) is rotated so the beams cross at the tumoura small sealed source is implanted in or next to the tumour — usually a beta or alpha emitter for its short range, sometimes a low-energy gamma emitter — or an isotope that collects in the organ is injected (iodine-131 for the thyroid)
Why that radiationgamma / X penetrate to a tumour deep in the bodya short-range emitter keeps the dose in the tumour; an implanted gamma source sits where the tumour is, so it too irradiates mainly the tumour
Rotationhealthy tissue along any one path gets only a fraction of the dose; the tumour, where all the beams meet, gets it all—
Healthy tissuesome damage to tissue the beams pass through (side effects)less damage to surrounding tissue; very targeted
Downsidesmany sessions; not all of the dose reaches the tumourneeds surgery or injection; the patient is contaminated (radioactive) for a time; source must have a suitable half-life

The June 2024 scheme (Q4(a)): of gamma, X-rays, radio waves and microwaves, gamma is the one that can be applied internally (from an implanted source); the others are applied externally.

parts.title: Why rotate the beam
parts.question: In external radiotherapy the gamma beam is rotated around the patient, always pointing at the tumour. Explain why. (2 marks)
steps: Tumour: the tumour is at the centre of rotation, so it is in the beam all the time and receives the full dose, enough to kill its cells.
Healthy tissue: each part of the healthy tissue is in the beam only briefly as it passes, so each gets a small dose and is less damaged.

questions.text: Compare the treatment of a tumour using an external gamma source with treatment using an implanted beta source. (4)
questions.model:
4 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1External howGamma beams from outside, penetrating to the tumour, rotated so they cross at it.
2External costThe beams pass through healthy tissue, which is damaged (less so with rotation); no surgery.
3Internal howA beta source placed in the tumour; beta's short range keeps the dose in the tumour.
4Internal costNeeds surgery / injection; the patient is radioactive for a time; less damage to surrounding tissue.

questions.text: Why is a short-range emitter (beta or alpha) a good choice for a source implanted in a tumour?
options: Its short range keeps the radiation within the tumour, sparing healthy tissue
questions.explain: Short range = dose stays local. (Sealed gamma sources are also implanted — gamma is the spec's answer for a radiation that can be applied internally.)

questions.text: Explain why gamma rays or X-rays, not alpha particles, are used for external radiotherapy. (2)
questions.model:
• Alpha is stopped by the skin (a few cm of air), so from outside it could never reach a tumour inside the body.
  • Gamma and X-rays penetrate deep into the body to reach the tumour.

questions.text: Iodine-131 (a beta emitter, half-life 8 days) is swallowed to treat thyroid cancer. Explain why this works and why the half-life is suitable. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1TargetingThe thyroid absorbs iodine, so the source collects in the tumour.
2BetaBeta has a short range in tissue, so it kills the thyroid cells while sparing the rest of the body.
3Half-life8 days is long enough to deliver the dose but short enough that the patient is not radioactive for months.

Describe internal treatment (a short-range beta or alpha source, or a sealed gamma source, implanted or injected)

sections.blurb: Ionising radiation kills cells, so it can kill a tumour. From outside, beams of gamma or X-rays are aimed through the body; from inside, a small source is put into or next to the tumour. Each has a cost.

sections.title: PET scanners and tracers

parts.title: How PET works, and the half-life problem
parts.html:
1. The patient is injected with a tracer containing a positron (β⁺) emitter — usually fluorine-18 attached to glucose (FDG), half-life about 110 minutes.
  2. The tracer collects where the body uses most glucose: active tissue such as a tumour or a working part of the brain.
  3. Each emitted positron meets an electron within a millimetre and the two annihilate: their mass becomes energy as two gamma rays travelling in opposite directions (180° apart).
  4. A ring of gamma detectors around the patient records the two gamma rays arriving at almost the same time on opposite sides; the decay happened on the line between them, and the small time difference says where along the line.
  5. Millions of such lines are combined by a computer into a 3-D image of where the tracer is concentrated.

These are the June 2024 marks (Q4(b)(i)): annihilate; two gamma rays; opposite directions; detected (gamma camera); at almost the same time; time difference gives the position. The June 2025 scheme for "positron meets electron" (Q4(b)(ii), 2 marks): any two of collide, annihilate, release (a pair of) gamma rays; "meet", "combine", "interact", "attract" and "light" were ignored.

Why made nearby (6.35P): positron emitters have short half-lives (F-18 110 min, others minutes), so the activity decays rapidly; if it were transported far it would be too weak to use by the time it arrived. So they are made in a cyclotron at or near the hospital and used within hours.

parts.title: The two gamma rays
parts.question: Explain how a PET scanner locates where a positron was emitted. (3 marks)
steps: Annihilation: the positron meets an electron and they annihilate, producing two gamma rays in opposite directions.
Detection: the two gamma rays reach detectors on opposite sides of the ring at almost the same time, so the emission was somewhere on the straight line joining those two detectors.
Position: the difference in arrival times gives where along the line; many lines crossing build the image.

questions.text: Describe what happens when a positron meets an electron. (2)
questions.model:
• They collide and annihilate (both are destroyed; their mass becomes energy)…
  • …producing two gamma rays travelling in opposite directions.

questions.text: Explain why isotopes used in PET scanners have to be produced close to the hospital. (2)
questions.model:
• They have very short half-lives, so their activity decays rapidly.
  • If transported a long way they would be too weak to use (have decayed) on arrival, so they are made in a nearby cyclotron and used within hours.

questions.text: Why are the gamma rays from annihilation detected in pairs on opposite sides of the patient?
options: Momentum is conserved: the two gamma rays leave in opposite directions
Gamma rays always come in pairs
questions.explain: Opposite directions from a near-stationary pair; detecting both fixes a line through the source.

questions.text: Explain why a positron emitter is used for PET rather than a gamma-emitting tracer such as technetium-99m. (2)
questions.model:
• Annihilation gives two gamma rays in opposite directions, so the source can be located on a line between two detectors — far more precise than a single gamma ray of unknown direction.
  • Positron emitters can be attached to glucose, so the image shows how active tissue is (metabolism), not just where it is.

questions.text: A hospital 300 km from the nearest cyclotron wants to use fluorine-18 (half-life 110 minutes). A delivery takes 5.5 hours. Calculate the fraction of the activity that would remain, and comment. (3)
questions.model:
• $5.5\ \text{h} = 330$ min $= 3$ half-lives.
  • Fraction remaining $= \dfrac{1}{2^{3}} = \dfrac{1}{8}$ (12.5%).
  • So seven-eighths has decayed before use: the dose injected would have to be eight times larger, or the hospital needs its own cyclotron.

Explain why PET isotopes must be produced close to the scanner
Explain how a tracer is chosen (where it collects, radiation, half-life)
sections.blurb: A PET scan injects a positron emitter. Each positron meets an electron and the pair annihilates into two gamma rays flying off in opposite directions; detecting both pins down where the decay happened. The isotope's half-life is so short it has to be made next door.

sections.title: Fission, the chain reaction and the reactor

parts.title: Fission and the chain
parts.html:
Fission (6.38P): a U-235 nucleus absorbs a slow neutron, becomes unstable (U-236), and splits into two smaller daughter nuclei plus two or three neutrons, releasing energy — mostly as kinetic energy of the fragments. Nuclear reactions (fission, fusion and radioactive decay) are all energy sources (6.37P).

Chain reaction (6.39P): the neutrons released can be absorbed by other U-235 nuclei, causing further fissions, which release more neutrons, and so on. Uncontrolled (every neutron causes another fission): the rate grows exponentially — a bomb. Controlled (on average exactly one neutron from each fission causes another): a steady rate of energy release — a reactor.

The June 2025 report (Q4(c)) wanted a "well-structured explanation" of what happens when one neutron meets one uranium nucleus: absorbed → unstable → splits into two daughter nuclei → releases neutrons → releases energy.

parts.title: Inside the reactor
parts.html:
PartJobWhy
Fuel rodscontain the uranium (enriched in U-235)
Moderator (graphite or water)slows down the fast neutrons released by fissionslow neutrons are far more likely to be absorbed by U-235 and cause fission; fast ones mostly bounce off
Control rods (boron or cadmium)absorb neutrons; raised or lowered to change how many are absorbedfewer neutrons → fewer fissions: this controls the rate of the chain reaction (and can shut it down)
Coolant (water or gas)carries the thermal energy out of the corethe kinetic energy of the fission fragments heats the fuel; the coolant transfers it to the boiler
Boiler, turbine, generatorheat makes steam, steam turns a turbine, the turbine turns a generatorthe same as any thermal power station from here on
Concrete and steel shieldingabsorbs the radiation from the corethe fission products are radioactive (6.42P), with long half-lives

Moderator vs control rods is the examiner's recurring complaint: in 2022 "most candidates did not recognise that control rods absorb neutrons" and confused them with the moderator. Moderator slows; control rods absorb. The June 2023 6-marker on this (Q10(c)): the indicative content has three strands — chain reaction, control rods, moderator — so cover all three: "neutrons hit other U-235 nuclei; control rods absorb neutrons to reduce the number of fissions; the moderator slows neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission".

The energy chain (2022 Q4(b)(iii), "few gained both marks"): nuclear store of the fuel → kinetic energy of the fission fragments → thermal store of the fuel and coolant (by heating) → steam → kinetic energy of the turbine → generator (electrically). Start with the fragments, not the coolant.

parts.title: The 6-marker, in order
parts.question: Explain how a chain reaction in a nuclear reactor is controlled, including the roles of the moderator and the control rods. (6 marks)
steps: Fission: a U-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two daughter nuclei, releasing two or three neutrons and energy.
Chain reaction: those neutrons can be absorbed by other U-235 nuclei, causing further fissions; left alone the number of fissions would grow rapidly.
Moderator: the neutrons are released fast; the moderator (graphite / water) slows them down, because slow neutrons are much more likely to be absorbed by U-235 and cause fission.
Control rods: made of boron, they absorb neutrons; lowering them further into the core absorbs more neutrons, so fewer fissions happen.
Controlled: the rods are set so that, on average, exactly one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another — a steady rate of energy release; pushing them fully in stops the reaction.
Energy out: the energy heats the coolant, which makes steam for the turbine and generator.

questions.text: Describe what happens when a neutron is absorbed by a uranium-235 nucleus. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1UnstableThe nucleus becomes unstable (uranium-236)…
2Splits…and splits into two smaller (daughter) nuclei…
3Neutrons + energy…releasing two or three neutrons and energy (mostly kinetic energy of the fragments).

questions.text: Explain the difference between the moderator and the control rods in a nuclear reactor. (2)
questions.model:
• The moderator slows down the neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission.
  • The control rods absorb neutrons, so fewer fissions occur — they set the rate of the chain reaction.

questions.text: What does "controlled chain reaction" mean?
options: On average one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission
questions.explain: Exactly one on average → steady rate; more than one → runaway; less than one → dies out.

questions.text: Describe how the energy released by fission in a reactor is used to generate electricity. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1Fragments → heatThe kinetic energy of the fission fragments heats the fuel; the coolant carries this thermal energy out of the core.
2SteamThe hot coolant heats water to make steam…
3Turbine…which turns a turbine connected to a generator.

questions.text: Explain why the waste from a nuclear reactor must be stored securely for a very long time. (2)
questions.model:
• The fission products are radioactive, many with long half-lives.
  • So they stay dangerous (ionising, causing cell damage and cancer) for thousands of years and must be kept from contaminating the environment.

questions.text: What would happen if the control rods were pulled fully out of the core?
options: More than one neutron per fission would cause further fissions and the rate would rise out of control
questions.explain: Nothing absorbing neutrons → an uncontrolled chain reaction.

questions.text: Explain why fast neutrons must be slowed down in a reactor. (2)
questions.model:
• A U-235 nucleus is much more likely to absorb a slow neutron than a fast one (fast ones tend to pass by or bounce off).
  • So without a moderator too few neutrons would cause fission and the chain reaction would die out.

sections.blurb: A slow neutron splits a uranium-235 nucleus into two smaller nuclei and two or three more neutrons, releasing energy. Those neutrons can split more nuclei: a chain reaction. A reactor keeps it going at a steady rate and turns the energy into electricity.

sections.title: Fusion: stars, conditions, and why it is hard on Earth

parts.title: Fusion, fission, and the obstacle
parts.html:
Fusion (6.43P): two small nuclei (e.g. hydrogen isotopes) join to form a larger nucleus (helium). The product has slightly less mass than the parts; the lost mass is released as energy. This is the energy source of stars, including the Sun. The June 2025 report: "the most common errors were to use the words 'atoms' or 'particles' instead of 'nuclei'". Say nuclei.

FissionFusion
Whata large nucleus splits into two smaller onestwo small nuclei join into a larger one
Started byabsorbing a neutronextreme temperature and pressure
Fueluranium-235, plutoniumhydrogen isotopes (deuterium, tritium)
Productsradioactive daughter nuclei, neutronshelium (not radioactive), neutrons
Wherereactors, bombsstars; experimental reactors
Energy per kg of fuelvery largeeven larger

Why it needs high temperature and pressure (6.45P): nuclei are positively charged, so they repel each other electrostatically. To get close enough to fuse they need enough kinetic energy to overcome that repulsion — moving extremely fast (very high temperature, millions of kelvin) — and must be crowded close together (very high pressure / density). At low temperature and pressure they never get near enough. The schemes mark "high energy" and "to overcome the (force of) repulsion" as separate points (June 2018 Q10(a)(i), Nov 2020 Q4(c)).

$E = mc^2$ is not on the equation list but has been supplied in five of the nine series (2018, 2019, 2023, 2024, 2025): the mass lost in fusion becomes energy. Rearrange to $m = E \div c^2$ with $c = 3.0 \times 10^8$ m/s. June 2025 Q10(b)(ii): the Sun radiates $3.9 \times 10^{26}$ J each second, so $m = 3.9 \times 10^{26} \div (3.0 \times 10^8)^2 = 4.3 \times 10^9$ kg each second — the unit was part of the evaluation mark ("$4.3 \times 10^9$ with no unit or the wrong unit scores 1 mark"), and every year's guidance says a power-of-ten slip costs the last mark only.

Why no fusion power station yet (6.46P): those conditions are very hard to create and contain on Earth — no material can hold a gas at millions of degrees, so it is confined by magnetic fields; so far the energy put in to reach the conditions is about as much as the energy got out, so it is not yet practical or economic.

parts.title: Why stars fuse and we struggle
parts.question: Explain why fusion happens in the core of the Sun but is difficult to achieve on Earth. (4 marks)
steps: Repulsion: nuclei are positively charged and repel each other, so they only fuse if they have enough energy to overcome that repulsion (collide at very high speed) and are packed close together.
In the Sun: gravity compresses the core to an enormous pressure and temperature (about 15 million K), so hydrogen nuclei move fast enough and are close enough to fuse.
On Earth: reaching those temperatures takes a huge energy input, and the hot plasma must be contained without touching any material (magnetic confinement).
Economics: so far the energy needed to create the conditions is about the same as the energy released, so it is not yet a practical, economic power source.

questions.text: Describe what is meant by nuclear fusion. (2)
questions.model:
• Two small nuclei join (fuse) to form a larger nucleus…
  • …with a loss of mass that is released as energy.

questions.text: Explain why nuclear fusion does not happen at low temperatures and pressures. (2)
questions.model:
• Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other (electrostatic repulsion between the protons).
  • A very high temperature gives the nuclei enough kinetic energy to overcome the repulsion, and a high pressure keeps them close together, so they get near enough to fuse (June 2018 Q10(a)(i): "high energy (1) to overcome (force of) repulsion (1)").

questions.text: Which statement about fusion and fission is correct?
options: Fission splits a large nucleus; fusion joins small nuclei
Fusion is the energy source of nuclear power stations today
Fission is the energy source of stars
questions.explain: Stars fuse; power stations (so far) fission.

questions.text: Give two differences between nuclear fusion and nuclear fission. (2)
questions.model:
• Fusion joins small nuclei; fission splits a large nucleus.
  • Fusion needs very high temperature and pressure to start; fission is started by a nucleus absorbing a neutron. (Or: fission products are radioactive; fusion's helium is not.)

questions.text: Explain why a fusion power station has not yet been built as a practical source of electricity. (2)
questions.model:
• The temperature and pressure needed are extremely hard to produce and contain on Earth (no container can touch plasma at millions of degrees; magnetic confinement is needed).
  • The energy required to reach those conditions has so far been about as much as the energy released, so it is not yet economic.

questions.text: A student writes: "In fusion, two hydrogen atoms join to make a helium atom." Correct the statement. (1)
questions.model: • It is the nuclei that fuse: two hydrogen nuclei join to form a helium nucleus, releasing energy.

Explain why fusion needs high temperature and pressure (electrostatic repulsion between protons)
Compare fusion and fission
Relate the conditions for fusion to the difficulty of a practical fusion power station
sections.blurb: Fusion is small nuclei joining into a larger one, losing a little mass that becomes a lot of energy. It powers stars. It needs enormous temperatures and pressures because the nuclei repel each other, which is why nobody has yet built a fusion power station that pays.

sections.title: Nuclear power: the for-and-against question

parts.title: For, against, decide
parts.html:
AdvantagesDisadvantages
No carbon dioxide (or other greenhouse gas) produced while generating — does not add to climate changeThe waste is radioactive, with long half-lives: it must be stored securely for thousands of years, and nobody has a permanent solution agreed
Reliable: generates continuously regardless of weather, unlike wind and solarVery expensive to build and to decommission (dismantle safely) at the end of its life
Enormous energy per kilogram of fuel: a small volume of fuel for a huge output, so little mining and transportRisk of accidents releasing radioactive material over a wide area (contamination lasting decades)
Fuel is relatively plentiful and not concentrated in a few countriesUranium is non-renewable; mining and enrichment have their own impacts and energy cost
Small land area compared with wind or solar farmsSecurity concerns: fuel and waste could be misused; public opposition

The shape of a Level-3 evaluate answer: at least two advantages and two disadvantages, each with the physics reason ("no CO₂ because the energy comes from fission, not combustion"; "waste is dangerous because the fission products are radioactive with long half-lives"), then a conclusion that follows: e.g. "nuclear is a good way to supply reliable low-carbon electricity while renewables are built up, provided the waste is stored securely". The Nov 2020 indicative content also credits: running out of fossil fuels; low running costs; large power output compared with wind or solar; fuel lasts hundreds of years with reprocessing; against — contamination of ground water, loss of life in an accident, terrorism.

parts.title: A compact evaluation
parts.question: Discuss the arguments for and against using nuclear power to meet the increasing demand for electricity. (6 marks)
steps: For 1: fission releases energy without burning fuel, so no carbon dioxide is produced during generation — it does not contribute to climate change as fossil fuels do.
For 2: a nuclear station runs continuously whatever the weather, so it provides a reliable baseload that wind and solar cannot; and a tiny mass of fuel gives a huge energy output.
Against 1: the fission products are radioactive with long half-lives, so the waste must be stored safely for thousands of years and there is no agreed permanent solution.
Against 2: stations are very expensive to build and decommission, and an accident could contaminate a large area for decades.

Judgement: because the climate problem is urgent and renewables are intermittent, nuclear power is a reasonable part of a low-carbon mix — provided the waste is dealt with properly and the high costs are accepted; it is not a complete answer on its own because the fuel is non-renewable.
