Every point is a fact plus a so: "no carbon emissions, so it does not add to global warming". Add a conclusion when the command word is discuss or evaluate; the marks are in the reasoned points.

facts.q: Structure of the atom?
facts.a: A tiny, dense, positive nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons orbiting at set distances. Almost all the mass is in the nucleus; most of the atom is empty space.

facts.q: Size of an atom? Of the nucleus?
facts.a: Atom about 10⁻¹⁰ m; nucleus about 10⁻¹⁵ m (1/10 000 of the atom).

facts.q: Relative masses and charges: p, n, e, e⁺?
facts.a: Proton 1, +1. Neutron 1, 0. Electron 1/1836, −1. Positron 1/1836, +1.

facts.q: Why is an atom neutral?
facts.a: Equal numbers of protons (+1) and electrons (−1).

facts.q: A and Z?
facts.a: A = mass (nucleon) number = protons + neutrons; Z = atomic (proton) number = protons. Neutrons = A − Z.

facts.q: Isotopes?
facts.a: Same element (same protons), different numbers of neutrons (different mass number).

facts.q: How does an electron move to a higher orbit?
facts.a: By absorbing electromagnetic radiation; it emits EM radiation when it falls back.

facts.q: How does an atom become a positive ion?
facts.a: It loses an outer electron (e.g. knocked out by ionising radiation), leaving more protons than electrons.

facts.q: Alpha particle?
facts.a: A helium nucleus: 2 protons + 2 neutrons, charge +2. Most ionising; stopped by paper or a few cm of air.

facts.q: Beta-minus particle?
facts.a: A fast electron from the nucleus (a neutron became a proton), charge −1. Stopped by a few mm of aluminium.

facts.q: Gamma ray?
facts.a: Electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus: no mass, no charge. Least ionising; reduced by thick lead or concrete.

facts.q: Penetration order? Ionising order?
facts.a: Penetration: alpha < beta < gamma. Ionising: alpha > beta > gamma.

facts.q: Sources of background radiation?
facts.a: Radon gas from rocks (largest), rocks and buildings, food and drink, cosmic rays, medical X-rays, nuclear industry (tiny).

facts.q: Two detectors of radiation?
facts.a: Geiger–Müller tube with a counter (count rate); photographic film, which darkens (film badges).

facts.q: Corrected count rate?
facts.a: Measured count rate − background count rate. Measure background with no source, over several minutes, repeat and average.

facts.q: Alpha decay: effect on A and Z?
Beta-minus decay: what happens, effect on A and Z?
facts.a: Neutron → proton + electron (emitted). A same, $Z + 1$.

facts.q: Beta-plus decay: what happens, effect on A and Z?
facts.a: Proton → neutron + positron (emitted). A same, $Z - 1$.

facts.q: Gamma emission: effect on A and Z?
facts.a: None — same element. The nucleus rearranges, loses energy and becomes more stable, often just after an alpha or beta decay.

facts.q: Neutron emission: effect on A and Z?
facts.a: A − 1, Z same.

facts.q: How do you check a nuclear equation?
facts.a: Top numbers (mass) add up on both sides; bottom numbers (charge) add up on both sides.

facts.q: Activity and its unit?
facts.a: Number of decays per second; becquerel (Bq) = 1 decay per second.

facts.q: Half-life (two forms)?
facts.a: Time for half the undecayed nuclei to decay; time for the activity to fall to half.

facts.q: Random but predictable?
facts.a: Cannot predict which nucleus decays or when; but with huge numbers of nuclei the half-life predicts the activity of the sample.

facts.q: Fraction left after n half-lives?
Dangers of ionising radiation?
facts.a: Ionises atoms in cells: kills or damages cells (tissue damage, burns); damages DNA → mutations → cancer.

facts.q: Precautions for handling a source?
facts.a: Tongs, point away, lead-lined box, limit time, keep distance, no eating, wash hands.

facts.q: Precautions for radiographers?
facts.a: Lead apron / lead screen, leave the room, limit time, film badge to monitor dose.

facts.q: Irradiation?
facts.a: Exposure to radiation from an external source: does not make you radioactive; stops when the source is removed; can be shielded.

facts.q: Contamination?
facts.a: Radioactive material on or in the object: it stays radioactive, keeps emitting, hard to remove, cannot be shielded from inside.

facts.q: Worst radiation for irradiation? For contamination?
facts.a: Irradiation: gamma (penetrates). Contamination: alpha (most ionising, now inside).

facts.q: Smoke alarm: source and why?
facts.a: Americium-241, alpha, long half-life. Alpha ionises air so a current flows; smoke absorbs alpha, current falls, alarm. Alpha cannot escape the casing.

facts.q: Sterilising / irradiating food: source and why?
facts.a: Gamma, long half-life: penetrates packaging and kills microbes; the food is irradiated, not contaminated.

facts.q: Medical tracer: source and why?
facts.a: Gamma emitter (technetium-99m), short half-life (6 h): gamma escapes the body to the camera; weakly ionising; dose falls quickly.

facts.q: Thickness gauge: source and why?
facts.a: Beta, long half-life: partly absorbed by paper so the count changes with thickness; alpha all stopped, gamma all through; steady activity.

facts.q: Two-reason answer for choosing a source?
facts.a: One reason for the type (penetration / ionisation) and one for the half-life — each linked to the job.

facts.q: Short vs long half-life: danger?
facts.a: Short: high activity now, soon gone. Long: lower activity but the hazard lasts — long-term storage.

facts.q: Plum pudding model?
facts.a: A ball of positive charge with electrons embedded in it.

facts.q: Alpha scattering: three observations and conclusions?
facts.a: Most straight through → mostly empty space. Some deflected → positive nucleus. Very few bounced back → tiny, dense nucleus with most of the mass.

facts.q: Bohr's change to the model?
facts.a: Electrons in fixed orbits (energy levels) at set distances; they move between levels by absorbing or emitting EM radiation — which matched observations.

facts.q: Half-life from a graph with background?
facts.a: Subtract the background from the start value, halve the corrected count, add the background back, read the time.

facts.q: Working backwards?
facts.a: Original activity = later activity × 2ⁿ.

facts.q: Why is the radiographer protected but not the patient?
facts.a: The radiographer is exposed many times a day (large total dose); the patient has one exposure where the benefit outweighs the risk.

facts.q: External vs internal tumour treatment?
facts.a: External: gamma/X beams rotated to cross at the tumour; no surgery; some healthy tissue damaged. Internal: a source (short-range beta/alpha, or a sealed gamma source) placed in the tumour; targeted; needs surgery; patient radioactive for a while.

facts.q: PET scan in four steps?
facts.a: Positron-emitting tracer injected → positron meets electron and they annihilate → two gamma rays in opposite directions → ring of detectors locates the line; many lines make the image.

facts.q: Why are PET isotopes made nearby?
facts.a: Very short half-lives: the activity decays rapidly, so they would be too weak after a long journey.

facts.q: Fission of U-235?
facts.a: Absorbs a slow neutron → unstable → splits into two daughter nuclei + 2 or 3 neutrons + energy.

facts.q: Chain reaction? Controlled?
facts.a: Neutrons from one fission cause further fissions. Controlled: on average one neutron per fission goes on to cause another.

facts.q: Moderator vs control rods?
facts.a: Moderator (graphite/water) SLOWS neutrons so they are absorbed and cause fission. Control rods (boron) ABSORB neutrons to set the rate.

facts.q: Energy chain in a reactor?
facts.a: Kinetic energy of fission fragments → thermal store of fuel and coolant → steam → kinetic energy of turbine → generator.

facts.q: Fission products?
facts.a: Radioactive, with long half-lives — the waste problem.

facts.q: Fusion?
facts.a: Two small NUCLEI join to form a larger nucleus; mass is lost and released as energy. The energy source of stars.

facts.q: Why does fusion need high temperature and pressure?
facts.a: Nuclei are positive and repel; they need enough kinetic energy (high T) to overcome the repulsion and must be close together (high P).

facts.q: Why no fusion power station yet?
facts.a: The conditions are extremely hard to create and contain; so far the energy in is about equal to the energy out — not practical or economic.

facts.q: Fission vs fusion in one line each?
facts.a: Fission: large nucleus splits, started by a neutron, radioactive products. Fusion: small nuclei join, needs extreme T and P, powers stars.

facts.q: Nuclear power: two for, two against?
facts.a: For: no CO₂ in generation; reliable, huge energy per kg. Against: long-lived radioactive waste; expensive to build and decommission, accident risk.

facts.q: State what is meant by: isotopes.
facts.a: Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons.

facts.q: State what is meant by: atomic (proton) number.
facts.a: The number of protons in the nucleus.

facts.q: State what is meant by: mass (nucleon) number.
facts.a: The number of protons plus neutrons in the nucleus.

facts.q: State what is meant by: ion.
facts.a: An atom that has lost or gained electrons and so has a charge (positive if it has lost them).

facts.q: State what is meant by: ionising radiation.
facts.a: Radiation with enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms, forming ions.

facts.q: State what is meant by: alpha particle.
facts.a: A helium nucleus: two protons and two neutrons, charge +2.

facts.q: State what is meant by: beta-minus particle.
facts.a: A fast electron emitted from the nucleus when a neutron turns into a proton.

facts.q: State what is meant by: gamma ray.
facts.a: High-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus.

facts.q: State what is meant by: positron.
facts.a: The antiparticle of the electron: same mass, charge +1; emitted in β⁺ decay.

facts.q: State what is meant by: background radiation.
facts.a: Low-level ionising radiation that is always present in the environment (rocks, radon, cosmic rays, food, medical).

facts.q: State what is meant by: activity.
facts.a: The number of decays per second of a source, in becquerels (Bq).

facts.q: State what is meant by: becquerel.
facts.a: One decay per second.

facts.q: State what is meant by: half-life.
facts.a: The time for half the undecayed nuclei to decay (or for the activity to halve).

facts.q: State what is meant by: random (decay).
facts.a: It cannot be predicted which nucleus will decay or when.

facts.q: State what is meant by: count rate.
facts.a: The number of counts per second (or minute) recorded by a detector.

facts.q: State what is meant by: irradiation.
facts.a: Exposure to radiation from an external source; the object does not become radioactive.

facts.q: State what is meant by: contamination.
facts.a: Radioactive material getting on or in an object, which then stays radioactive.

facts.q: State what is meant by: nuclear fission.
facts.a: A large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei and neutrons, releasing energy (P).

facts.q: State what is meant by: nuclear fusion.
facts.a: Two small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus, with a loss of mass and a release of energy (P).

facts.q: State what is meant by: chain reaction.
facts.a: Neutrons from one fission go on to cause further fissions (P).

types.name: Protons, neutrons and nucleons from a nuclide
equations: mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons
number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number
types.method: The atomic number (the lower number in the symbol) is the number of protons. The mass number (the upper number) is the total number of nucleons, protons plus neutrons. So neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but different mass numbers, so they differ only in the number of neutrons.
commonErrors: Giving the mass number as the number of neutrons
Subtracting the wrong way round, or adding the two numbers
Thinking isotopes have different numbers of protons: it is the number of neutrons that changes

worked.question: A nucleus of carbon-14 has mass number 14 and atomic number 6. How many neutrons does the nucleus contain?
steps: Known: mass number = 14, atomic number = 6. Unknown: number of neutrons.
number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number
number of neutrons = 14 − 6
number of neutrons = 8

practice.question: A nucleus of sodium-23 has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. How many protons does the nucleus contain?
practice.hint: The atomic number is the number of protons.
walkthrough: The atomic number is the number of protons.

practice.question: A nucleus of uranium-238 has mass number 238 and atomic number 92. How many nucleons does the nucleus contain?
practice.hint: Nucleons means protons and neutrons together, which is the mass number.
walkthrough: The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons).

practice.question: Iodine-131 is used in medicine. Its nucleus has mass number 131 and atomic number 53. How many neutrons does the nucleus contain?
practice.hint: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

practice.question: A nucleus of cobalt contains 27 protons and 33 neutrons. What is the mass number of this nucleus?
practice.hint: Mass number = protons + neutrons.

practice.question: Chlorine has atomic number 17 and two common isotopes, chlorine-35 (mass number 35) and chlorine-37 (mass number 37). How many more neutrons does a chlorine-37 nucleus have than a chlorine-35 nucleus?
practice.hint: Work out the neutrons in each isotope (mass number − 17), then subtract.

practice.question: A nucleus of lead-206 has mass number 206 and atomic number 82. How many more neutrons than protons does the nucleus contain?
practice.hint: Find the number of neutrons first (206 − 82), then compare it with the number of protons.

types.name: Balancing nuclear equations
equations: alpha decay: mass number − 4, atomic number − 2
beta-minus decay: mass number unchanged, atomic number + 1
types.method: The mass numbers must add up to the same total on both sides of a nuclear equation, and so must the atomic numbers. An alpha particle is a helium nucleus (mass number 4, atomic number 2), so the daughter nucleus has a mass number 4 lower and an atomic number 2 lower. A beta-minus particle is an electron (mass number 0, atomic number −1), so the mass number stays the same and the atomic number goes up by 1.
commonErrors: Taking 2 off the mass number in alpha decay instead of 4
Lowering the atomic number by 1 in beta-minus decay instead of raising it by 1
Changing the mass number in beta decay: the electron has mass number 0

worked.question: Radium-226 (mass number 226, atomic number 88) decays by emitting an alpha particle to form a nucleus of radon. What is the mass number of the radon nucleus?
steps: Known: parent mass number 226, alpha particle mass number 4. Unknown: daughter mass number.
Mass numbers balance: 226 = (daughter mass number) + 4
daughter mass number = 226 − 4
mass number of radon = 222

practice.question: Uranium-238 (mass number 238, atomic number 92) decays by emitting an alpha particle to form a nucleus of thorium. What is the atomic number of the thorium nucleus?
practice.hint: An alpha particle carries away 2 protons, so the atomic number falls by 2.

practice.question: Carbon-14 (mass number 14, atomic number 6) decays by emitting a beta-minus particle to form a nucleus of nitrogen. What is the atomic number of the nitrogen nucleus?
practice.hint: A beta-minus particle has atomic number −1, so the daughter's atomic number must be 1 higher to balance.

practice.question: Polonium-210 (mass number 210, atomic number 84) decays by emitting an alpha particle to form a nucleus of lead. What is the mass number of the lead nucleus?
practice.hint: The alpha particle takes away 4 nucleons.

practice.question: Strontium-90 (mass number 90, atomic number 38) decays by emitting a beta-minus particle to form a nucleus of yttrium. What is the atomic number of the yttrium nucleus?
practice.hint: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton, so the atomic number goes up by 1.

practice.question: Thorium-232 (mass number 232, atomic number 90) emits an alpha particle. The nucleus formed then emits a beta-minus particle. What is the atomic number of the nucleus after both decays?
practice.hint: Do the decays one at a time: alpha takes 2 off the atomic number, then beta-minus adds 1.
walkthrough: after the alpha decay: atomic number = 90 − 2 = 88
after the beta-minus decay: atomic number = 88 + 1

practice.question: Uranium-238 (mass number 238, atomic number 92) decays through a series of alpha and beta-minus decays to radon-222 (mass number 222, atomic number 86). How many alpha particles are emitted in this series?
practice.hint: Only alpha decays change the mass number, by 4 each time; compare the two mass numbers.
walkthrough: Beta-minus decays do not change the mass number.

types.name: Half-life: fraction and activity remaining
types.method: Each half-life halves what is left. Work out how many half-lives fit in the time (time ÷ half-life, in matching units), then halve the starting activity, count rate or number of nuclei that many times. Give a fraction as a decimal (1/4 = 0.25) unless the question asks for an activity or a count rate.
commonErrors: Dividing by the number of half-lives (÷ 3) instead of halving three times (÷ 8)
Counting the half-lives with the time in the wrong unit (hours against minutes)
Giving the amount that has decayed when the question asks for the amount remaining, or the other way round

worked.question: A radioactive source has an activity of 800 Bq. Its half-life is 2 hours. Calculate the activity of the source after 6 hours.
steps: Known: starting activity 800 Bq, half-life 2 h, time 6 h. Unknown: activity after 6 h.
number of half-lives = 6 / 2 = 3
activity = 100 Bq

practice.question: What fraction of the radioactive nuclei in a sample remain undecayed after 2 half-lives? Give your answer as a decimal.
practice.hint: Halve 1 twice.

practice.question: A source in a school laboratory has an activity of 1200 Bq. Calculate its activity after 2 half-lives.
practice.hint: Halve 1200 twice.

practice.question: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. A sample gives a count rate of 640 counts/min. Calculate the count rate from the sample after 24 days.
practice.hint: Find the number of half-lives (24 ÷ 8) first, then halve 640 that many times.

practice.question: Technetium-99m, used in medical imaging, has a half-life of 6 hours. What fraction of the technetium-99m injected into a patient remains after 1 day? Give your answer as a decimal.
practice.hint: Change 1 day into hours before counting the half-lives.
walkthrough: 1 day = 24 hours, so number of half-lives = 24 / 6 = 4

practice.question: A radioactive gas has a half-life of 20 minutes. A sample of the gas has an activity of 3200 Bq. Calculate the activity of the sample after 2 hours.
practice.hint: Change 2 hours into minutes, divide by 20 to count the half-lives, then halve 3200 that many times.

practice.question: A sample contains 2400 undecayed nuclei of a radon isotope with a half-life of 55 s. How many of these nuclei have decayed after 165 s?
practice.hint: Find how many remain after 165 ÷ 55 half-lives, then subtract from 2400.

types.name: Half-life: counting half-lives and finding times
equations: number of half-lives = how many times the activity halves
time taken = number of half-lives × half-life
half-life = time taken / number of half-lives
types.method: Halve the starting value again and again until you reach the final value, and count the halvings: that is the number of half-lives. Multiply by the half-life to get the time taken, or divide the time taken by the number of half-lives to find the half-life itself. Keep the units consistent: a half-life in minutes gives a time in minutes.
commonErrors: Dividing the start by the finish and calling that the number of half-lives (1600 / 200 = 8 means 3 half-lives, not 8)
Mixing hours and minutes between the half-life and the time taken
Counting the starting value as the first half-life

worked.question: The activity of a source falls from 1600 Bq to 200 Bq. The half-life of the source is 4 hours. Calculate the time this takes.
steps: Known: 1600 Bq falls to 200 Bq, half-life 4 h. Unknown: time taken.
time = 3 × 4
time = 12 hours

practice.question: The activity of a radioactive source falls from 800 Bq to 50 Bq. How many half-lives have passed?
practice.hint: Keep halving 800 until you reach 50 and count the halvings.

practice.question: A source used in a hospital has a half-life of 30 minutes. Its count rate falls from 6000 counts/s to 750 counts/s. Calculate the time this takes.
practice.hint: Count the halvings from 6000 to 750, then multiply by 30 minutes.

practice.question: The activity of a source falls from 400 Bq to 50 Bq in 36 minutes. Calculate the half-life of the source.
practice.hint: Count the halvings, then divide 36 minutes by that number.

practice.question: The count rate from a sample falls from 2400 counts/min to 300 counts/min in 2 hours. Calculate the half-life of the sample in minutes.
practice.hint: Change 2 hours into minutes, count the halvings, then divide.

practice.question: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. A bone found at a dig contains one eighth of the carbon-14 it had when the animal died. Calculate the age of the bone.
practice.hint: How many halvings take 1 down to 1/8? Multiply that by 5730 years.

practice.question: A detector reading from a short-lived source falls from 1920 counts/s to 120 counts/s in 1 minute 20 seconds. Calculate the half-life of the source in seconds.
practice.hint: Change 1 minute 20 seconds into seconds, count the halvings from 1920 to 120, then divide.

types.name: Count rate with background
equations: corrected count rate = measured count rate − background count rate
types.method: A detector always records some background radiation, so subtract the background count rate from every reading before using half-life ideas; the corrected count rate is what the source alone gives. Then halve, count half-lives or find a time exactly as before. If the question asks what the detector will read, add the background back on at the end.
commonErrors: Halving the measured count rate without taking the background off first
Subtracting the background from the starting reading but not from the final one
Forgetting to add the background back on when the question asks what the detector reads
Background given per hour while the readings are per minute: convert it first

worked.question: With a source in front of it, a detector reads 540 counts/min. The background count rate is 40 counts/min. The half-life of the source is 10 minutes. Calculate the corrected count rate from the source after 20 minutes.
steps: Known: measured 540 counts/min, background 40 counts/min, half-life 10 min, time 20 min.
corrected count rate now = 540 − 40 = 500 counts/min
number of half-lives = 20 / 10 = 2
corrected count rate = 125 counts/min

practice.question: A Geiger counter placed near a rock sample reads 275 counts/min. With the rock removed it reads 25 counts/min. Calculate the corrected count rate from the rock.
practice.hint: The reading with the rock removed is the background; subtract it.

practice.question: A detector near a source reads 650 counts/min. The background count rate is 50 counts/min and the half-life of the source is 15 minutes. What will the detector read after 15 minutes?
practice.hint: Take the background off, halve once, then add the background back on because the question asks for the detector reading.
walkthrough: after 1 half-life: 600 / 2 = 300 counts/min from the source

practice.question: The reading on a detector near a source falls from 1300 counts/min to 180 counts/min. The background count rate is 20 counts/min. How many half-lives have passed?
practice.hint: Subtract 20 from both readings before counting the halvings.

practice.question: The reading on a detector near a source falls from 820 counts/min to 120 counts/min in 30 minutes. The background count rate is 20 counts/min. Calculate the half-life of the source.
practice.hint: Correct both readings for background, count the halvings, then divide 30 minutes by that number.

practice.question: Before an experiment a student records 180 background counts in one hour. With a source present the detector reads 243 counts/min. The half-life of the source is 5 minutes. Calculate the corrected count rate from the source after 20 minutes.
practice.hint: Change the background into counts per minute first, subtract it, then halve for 20 ÷ 5 half-lives.

practice.question: A detector near a source reads 1030 counts/min. The background count rate is 30 counts/min and the half-life of the source is 8 days. Calculate how long it takes for the detector reading to fall to 155 counts/min.
practice.hint: Correct both the starting and the final reading for background, count the halvings, then multiply by 8 days.

types.name: Reading a decay graph
equations: half-life = time for the activity to halve
types.method: Find the starting activity (or count rate) where the curve meets the vertical axis, halve it, and read across to the curve and down to the time axis: that time is the half-life. Check it by halving again, which should take the same time. If there is a background line, measure the count rates from the background line, not from zero.
commonErrors: Reading the time when the activity reaches zero instead of the time to reach half of the starting value
Halving the time axis instead of the activity axis
Ignoring the background count rate line on a count-rate graph
Taking the end of the graph as the end of the decay: the curve never actually reaches zero

worked.question: The graph shows how the activity of a radioactive source changes with time. The dashed lines show the reading at half of the starting activity. Use the graph to find the half-life of the source.
steps: Starting activity (at t = 0) = 800 Bq.
Half of this is 400 Bq.
Reading across at 400 Bq and down to the time axis gives 20 s.
half-life = 20 s

graph.alt: Activity–time graph falling from 800 Bq at 0 s to 400 Bq at 20 s, with dashed lines marking that reading, and on to 25 Bq at 100 s

practice.question: The graph shows the count rate from a radioactive sample against time. Use the graph to find the half-life of the sample.
practice.hint: Read the count rate at t = 0, halve it, and find the time when the curve reaches that value.
walkthrough: The curve reaches 600 counts/minute at 15 minutes.

graph.alt: Count rate–time graph falling from 1200 counts per minute at 0 minutes to 600 at 15 minutes and on towards 19 at 90 minutes

practice.question: The graph shows the activity of a source against time. Point X marks the activity 60 s after the start. Use the graph to find the activity at X.
practice.hint: Go up from 60 s on the time axis to the curve, then read across to the activity axis.
walkthrough: X is at t = 60 s on the curve.
Reading across from X to the activity axis gives 200 Bq.

graph.alt: Activity–time graph falling from 800 Bq at 0 s to 200 Bq at the marked point X at 60 s, and on to 50 Bq at 120 s

practice.question: The graph shows the activity of a radioactive source against time. Use the graph to find how many half-lives occur in the first 40 minutes.
practice.hint: Find the half-life from the graph first (the time for 400 Bq to fall to 200 Bq), then divide 40 minutes by it.
walkthrough: Starting activity = 400 Bq; half of this is 200 Bq.
The curve reaches 200 Bq at 10 minutes, so the half-life is 10 minutes.

graph.alt: Activity–time graph falling from 400 Bq at 0 minutes to 200 Bq at 10 minutes and 25 Bq at 40 minutes

practice.question: The graph shows the count rate from a sample of a radioactive isotope against time. Use the graph to find how long it takes for the count rate to fall to 400 counts/s.
practice.hint: Read across from 400 counts/s to the curve, then down to the time axis.
walkthrough: 3200 → 1600 → 800 → 400 is 3 half-lives, and the curve shows each halving takes 4 hours.
The curve reaches 400 counts/s at 12 hours.

graph.alt: Count rate–time graph falling from 3200 counts per second at 0 hours to 1600 at 4 hours, 400 at 12 hours and 50 at 24 hours

practice.question: The graph shows the activity of a radioactive source during the first 40 minutes after it is prepared. Use the graph to find the half-life, then calculate the activity of the source 60 minutes after it is prepared.
practice.hint: Find the time for 6400 Bq to halve to 3200 Bq, work out how many of those half-lives fit in 60 minutes, then halve 6400 that many times.
walkthrough: Starting activity = 6400 Bq; the curve reaches 3200 Bq at 10 minutes, so the half-life is 10 minutes.

graph.alt: Activity–time graph falling from 6400 Bq at 0 minutes to 3200 Bq at 10 minutes and 400 Bq at 40 minutes

practice.question: The graph shows the reading on a detector placed near a radioactive source. The dashed line shows the background count rate, which was measured before the source was brought in. Use the graph to find the half-life of the source.
practice.hint: Subtract the background (100 counts/minute) from the starting reading, halve what is left, add the background back on, and find the time when the curve reaches that reading.
walkthrough: At t = 0 the detector reads 900 counts/minute; background = 100 counts/minute.
Count rate from the source alone = 900 − 100 = 800 counts/minute.
After one half-life the source gives 400 counts/minute, so the detector reads 400 + 100 = 500 counts/minute.
The curve reaches 500 counts/minute at 10 minutes.
